title: Weather forecasts are 95% accurate, and nobody believes them
dek: A meteorologist says forecasts are about 95% accurate in the three-to-five-day window, but the public only remembers the time it got rained on; climate isn't future tense, it's present continuous.
why: Medium information density: the first half is career explainer, the second half — on probability, hurricane cones and climate lag — is worth hearing.
who: Engineers and product people interested in meteorology, climate communication and probability communication; anyone doing risk communication, early-warning systems, agriculture or energy decisions.
skip: The first ten minutes of host monologue and guest résumé can be skipped.

points.h: The forecast isn't wrong, your memory is biased
points.body: The public broadly believes weather forecasts are often wrong, but the number Shepard gives is about 95% accuracy in the three-to-five-day window. The problem isn't the model, it's memory: people remember the times the barbecue got rained on, the times the kid's ballgame got rained on, and not all the days the forecast got it right. He uses the kicker analogy — perfect all season, misses one in the Super Bowl, and that's the only one anyone remembers. What this changes: forecast reliability is far higher than its public reputation, and that reputation is shaped by statistical bias.

points.h: Bomb cyclone isn't a new word, it's new exposure
points.body: Many people assume that terms like bomb cyclone, polar vortex and derecho are signals that the climate has changed. Shepard rejects that outright: these terms have existed in meteorology for decades, they've just recently come into heavy use in mass media. So you can't use the popularity of a term as an anchor for climate change. What is actually changing is intensity — stronger downpours, more frequent and more severe heat waves, rapid intensification of hurricanes, higher sea levels pushing more water in with the same storm, bigger storm-surge losses.

points.h: The reason for optimism is that we know what to do
points.body: Shepard says he doesn't want to stop at bad news, because the good news is this isn't a problem that still needs head-scratching research — we know what to do: cut carbon emissions, and we must adapt, because some of the change has already crossed irreversible points. He cites the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave: most homes there had no air conditioning, Canada recorded 120 degrees Fahrenheit, it was called a once-in-a-millennium event, but climate change made it 150 times more likely, causing nearly $9 billion in losses and 1,400 heat deaths. The adaptation strategy is to retrofit those houses with air conditioning.

points.h: Warming makes blizzards fiercer, not milder
points.body: The counterintuitive mechanism: hurricanes, downpours and blizzards all start with water vapor. The Clausius-Clapeyron equation says that a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapor. For every 1 degree Fahrenheit of warming, water vapor increases by about 4% (7% in Celsius). A century ago the Northeast U.S. averaged 22 degrees Fahrenheit in winter; now it's up to 26, and some years 30 — against 22 degrees that's a 32% increase in water vapor, and 30 degrees is still below the 32-degree freezing point. So a warmer planet means more water entering the atmosphere, and blizzards can hit harder.

points.h: The hurricane cone is probability, not a path
points.body: During Hurricane Ian in 2022, some people evacuated from one part of the cone to another, a complete misreading. What the cone means is: the storm center has a 67% chance of falling somewhere inside the cone, not that the storm will travel along the cone's center line. Shepard says the public broadly struggles with probability, uncertainty, more than two processes happening at once, and anything that can't be simplified to their level — so they simplify complex information down to their level, and the price is bad decisions.

points.h: A 20% chance of rain doesn't mean it won't rain
points.body: Shepard tells the story of getting rained on while floating a river with his son: a woman nearby complained that it was only a 20% chance of rain and meteorologists are always wrong. But that day wasn't 0% — they just happened to be in that 20% area. Statistically, 80% of the area stayed dry; they landed in the 20% that got rain. One way to compute POP is confidence of rain × fraction of area affected: if confidence is 60% and coverage is 60% of the area, POP is 36%. So "20% chance" doesn't mean "it won't rain" — it's describing a regional probability distribution.

points.h: Satellites cover more, balloons resolve finer
points.body: On the trade-off between weather balloons and satellites: satellites provide more consistent observations over a wider area, while balloons only have data at the launch point and launch time, sometimes only twice a day. But satellite resolution is far coarser. Shepard uses a phone camera analogy: more pixels make a better photo, and the finer the resolution of an observation or model, the more fine-scale weather it can capture. A thermometer or barometer at your location has far better resolution than the blurry one-square-mile reading a satellite gives you.
